heading: Cold open
narration: A Greenland shark is a large, heavy-bodied, slow-moving shark, grey to blackish-brown, with a short rounded snout, small eyes, two small dorsal fins and no anal fin.

heading: Cold open
narration: The longest one measured in a study published in the journal Science in 2016 was 502 centimetres from snout to tail.

heading: Cold open
narration: That number records one animal on one deck. It does not tell you what the species looks like alive, in darkness, far below the surface.

heading: Cold open

heading: Its body is built for slowness, not for pursuit

heading: Its body is built for slowness, not for pursuit
narration: The snout is short and rounded rather than pointed. The overall impression is less a torpedo than a heavy, slightly flattened log that happens to carry fins.

heading: Its body is built for slowness, not for pursuit
narration: The fins are where expectations break. On many familiar sharks, the first dorsal fin is a tall triangle you could pick out from a boat.

heading: Its body is built for slowness, not for pursuit
narration: A Greenland shark has two small dorsal fins, low and set well back, and neither dorsal fin carries a spine.

heading: Its body is built for slowness, not for pursuit
narration: There is no anal fin, a trait it shares with the dogfish-like sharks it is related to.

heading: Its body is built for slowness, not for pursuit
narration: The pectoral fins are modest for an animal this size. All of it points the same way, toward a body that is not built for speed.

heading: Its body is built for slowness, not for pursuit
narration: Tagging studies have recorded very slow cruising speeds, which fits. But whether shape alone proves a slow lifestyle is a separate question. Shape suggests. The tag records are what carry the weight.

heading: Its body is built for slowness, not for pursuit
narration: Colour is harder than it sounds. Described specimens run in a range from grey to blackish-brown, sometimes with paler patches, scars and scrapes.

narration: But colour in an image depends on the light it was made in.

heading: Its body is built for slowness, not for pursuit
narration: The same shark lifted onto a deck under an overcast sky, lit by a diver's lamp, or filmed under a deep-sea camera's lights can look like three different animals.

heading: Its body is built for slowness, not for pursuit
narration: Up close, the skin is rough. Like other sharks, it is covered in dermal denticles, small tooth-like scales.

heading: Its body is built for slowness, not for pursuit
narration: That is a family resemblance rather than a special feature, but it shapes what you see on camera: a matte surface that scatters light instead of shining.

heading: Its body is built for slowness, not for pursuit
narration: That is part of why these animals so often look dull, almost velvety, on footage.

heading: The eyes are small, and often not alone
narration: The eyes are small for the head and sit on its sides.

heading: The eyes are small, and often not alone
narration: As Smithsonian Ocean's overview of the deep sea explains, sunlight fades quickly with depth, and colours drop out one by one as the water absorbs them.

heading: The eyes are small, and often not alone
narration: In the darkness where much of this species lives, small eyes are not unusual. What is unusual is what is often hanging from them.

heading: The eyes are small, and often not alone
narration: Many Greenland sharks carry a copepod called Ommatokoita elongata. A copepod is a small crustacean, a relative of animals at the base of many ocean food webs, but this one has taken a parasitic path.

heading: The eyes are small, and often not alone
narration: It anchors itself into the surface of the eye and trails away from it as a pale, ribbon-like body.

heading: The eyes are small, and often not alone
narration: That is the detail most people remember once they have seen it.

heading: The eyes are small, and often not alone
narration: It is known the plain way: sharks examined in hand, the parasite removed and studied, and the same species found on eye after eye across many catches.

heading: The eyes are small, and often not alone
narration: Not every shark carries it, and how common it is varies between the places that have been sampled.

heading: The eyes are small, and often not alone
narration: The next claim usually made is that the parasite blinds the shark.

heading: The eyes are small, and often not alone
narration: Be careful here. Examinations have found damage to the surface of the eye where the parasite attaches, and it is reasonable to think vision suffers.

heading: The eyes are small, and often not alone
narration: But damage to the surface of the eye is not proof the shark is blind, and nobody has run an eye test on a free-swimming shark in deep water.

includes: damage to the surface of the eye

heading: The eyes are small, and often not alone
narration: Where little sunlight reaches, the practical cost of poorer vision is also hard to judge.

heading: The eyes are small, and often not alone
narration: The honest position is that some harm is likely, and the size of that harm is not settled.

heading: The teeth do two different jobs
narration: Open the mouth and the shark stops looking sluggish. The jaw holds two kinds of tooth.

args.title: Reading the jaw
args.conclusion: a grip above and a saw below

heading: The teeth do two different jobs
narration: Along the top sit narrow, pointed upper teeth, built to hold. Along the bottom sit broad, angled lower teeth whose cusps lean sideways and line up edge to edge, forming something close to a continuous cutting blade.

heading: The teeth do two different jobs
narration: Together they give a grip above and a saw below. The shark can clamp with the top jaw and work its head to slice with the bottom one.

args.title: Reading the jaw
args.conclusion: a grip above and a saw below

heading: The teeth do two different jobs
narration: That jaw is why stomach contents matter so much to this story.

heading: The teeth do two different jobs
narration: Greenland sharks caught by researchers and fishers have been found with fish, and sometimes with the remains of seals, in their stomachs.

heading: The teeth do two different jobs
narration: The teeth show the shark can cut large prey. They do not show whether that prey was hunted or scavenged, and for a body this slow, that question remains open.

heading: The teeth do two different jobs
narration: Appearance can tell you what an animal is equipped to do. It cannot tell you how often it does it.

narration: It becomes a cop-out when uncertainty is used selectively — enough evidence to make a dramatic claim, and suddenly not enough when someone asks them to defend it.

heading: Its size is measured; the biggest claims are not
narration: Size is where that warning applies most directly. A length that deserves trust comes from a simple sequence: land the animal, lay it straight, measure from snout to tail, and record who did it.

args.title: How a length becomes a record

heading: Its size is measured; the biggest claims are not
narration: In the 2016 Science study led by Julius Nielsen, the longest shark was a female at 502 centimetres, just over five metres.

heading: Its size is measured; the biggest claims are not
narration: That is a measured figure with a method behind it. It is not a claim about the maximum size the species can reach. It is only the largest animal in that sample.

args.title: How a length becomes a record

heading: Its size is measured; the biggest claims are not
narration: You will find larger figures in popular articles and older accounts. Some may be accurate.

heading: Its size is measured; the biggest claims are not
narration: But a repeated number with no specimen behind it is not the same as a measured specimen with a method, and this script cannot trace those larger figures to animals someone measured and recorded.

heading: Its size is measured; the biggest claims are not
narration: So you will not get a maximum here. Estimates vary, and the published record is thinner at the top end than the confident numbers online suggest.

heading: You cannot read its age from its appearance
narration: Here is a limit of looking that surprises most people. A Greenland shark gives you almost no visible clue to its age, and the growth bands used to age many other sharks are not usable in this species.

args.title: Eye lens dating
args.conclusion: an age estimate with a wide range

heading: You cannot read its age from its appearance
narration: Nielsen's team turned to the eye instead. The centre of the eye lens, the lens nucleus formed before birth, stays essentially unchanged for life.

heading: You cannot read its age from its appearance
narration: That tissue had its radiocarbon measured and compared with the bomb pulse, the spike in radiocarbon released by atmospheric nuclear weapons tests in the middle of the twentieth century, which marked ocean food webs.

args.title: Eye lens dating
args.conclusion: an age estimate with a wide range

heading: You cannot read its age from its appearance
narration: Sharks born after the spike carry its signal. Older ones do not.

heading: You cannot read its age from its appearance
narration: Combine that with body length, and you get an age estimate with a wide range.

args.title: Eye lens dating

heading: You cannot read its age from its appearance
narration: The width of that range is the point. In the Science study, the estimated age of the largest female, the 502 centimetre animal, was 392 years, with an uncertainty of 120 years either way, a range from 272 to 512 years.

args.caption: Estimated age of the largest female

heading: You cannot read its age from its appearance
narration: The study's headline in Science is that Greenland sharks live for at least 272 years.

heading: You cannot read its age from its appearance
narration: Notice what the method cannot do. It cannot look at a shark in a video and tell you its age.

args.caption: Estimated age of the largest female

heading: You cannot read its age from its appearance
narration: A long body suggests an old animal, but growth in the cold is so poorly known that two sharks of the same length could differ in age by a great deal.

heading: A photograph does not always name the species
narration: Everything so far assumes you know which shark you are looking at.

heading: A photograph does not always name the species
narration: Often you do not. The Greenland shark has a close relative, the Pacific sleeper shark, and the two look strikingly alike: the same heavy body, small fins, absent anal fin and muted colour.

heading: A photograph does not always name the species
narration: Genetic work has even reported animals with mixed ancestry where their ranges come near each other.

heading: A photograph does not always name the species
narration: So when a camera far from the Arctic films a large, slow, dark shark with small fins, the image is evidence of the genus, not proof of the species.

heading: A photograph does not always name the species
narration: Confirming the species usually takes more than a picture. It takes a body or tissue sample, genetic testing, and comparison with known specimens.

heading: A photograph does not always name the species
narration: Only then do you get a confident name. That is why so many descriptions of what a Greenland shark looks like lean on landed animals rather than live footage. Footage shows behaviour and setting. Specimens settle identity.

heading: What to notice in the edit
narration: As you watch, notice which images show dead animals and which show living ones.

heading: What to notice in the edit
narration: Landed sharks reveal proportions, fins and teeth clearly, but bodies sag out of water and eyes lose their shape.

heading: What to notice in the edit
narration: Living footage shows posture and slowness, but colour is at the mercy of the lights.

heading: What to notice in the edit
narration: Notice too where each number comes from. Science stands behind the length and age figures.

heading: What to notice in the edit
narration: Smithsonian Ocean stands behind how light fades with depth. Nothing on screen claims more than those sources do.

heading: Evidence limit
narration: This evidence settles the body plan, fins and teeth well, because those are visible on every landed animal and consistent across them.

heading: Evidence limit
narration: It settles that the eye parasite is a copepod. It does not establish the maximum size the species reaches, and it does not establish how colour varies across its range.

heading: Evidence limit
narration: It leaves open whether the parasite impairs vision in any meaningful way.

heading: Evidence limit
narration: And it cannot turn an image into an age. A careful description of this shark has edges, and the edges are part of the description.

heading: Closing
narration: So picture it plainly: a long, dark, heavy shark with a small head, small eyes, low fins and no anal fin, sometimes trailing a pale thread from one eye, armed with a jaw that grips above and cuts below.

heading: Closing
narration: Its appearance is well described. Its age, its limits and much of its life in the dark are still being measured.
